label: The body is a collective intelligence, so behavioural tools should beat micromanagement
claim: Levin's central hypothesis is that the body is a collective intelligence behaving in anatomical, physiological and transcriptional spaces, so behavioural-science tools developed to collaborate with complex systems should provide therapeutic advantages over biochemical micromanagement of molecular components.
quote: The central hypothesis is that the body is a collective intelligence behaving in anatomical, physiological, and transcriptional spaces [13]. Thus, behavioral science tools developed to collaborate with complex systems should provide therapeutic advantages over biochemical micromanagement.
scope: Human and animal bodies; biomedical and bioengineering interventions
measurable_quantities: therapeutic efficacy and durability of training- or setpoint-based interventions versus direct molecular interventions
rates of habituation and relapse after treatment
candidate_data: Comparative clinical-trial outcome data (e.g. ClinicalTrials.gov results) for conditioning-based versus standard dosing regimens; no dataset directly tests the general hypothesis.

label: Intelligence is reaching the same goal by different means, including in morphogenesis
claim: Levin defines intelligence, following William James, as the ability to reach the same goal by different means; for tissues this is the problem-solving competency to adapt to conditions in order to construct and repair a specific morphology or function, a functional definition that lets intelligence be studied in non-neural substrates.
quote: I define intelligence here in William James’ [22] sense as the ability to reach the same goal by different means: the focus is on problem‐solving competency, which in this case is the ability to adapt to conditions to construct and repair a specific morphology or function.
scope: Any biological system, from molecular networks to organisms
candidate_data: none known

label: Gene regulatory network models show habituation, sensitization and Pavlovian learning
claim: When standard behavioural-training protocols are applied to even simple models of gene regulatory networks and molecular pathways, the models show habituation, sensitization and Pavlovian (associative) conditioning, a dynamical state memory that requires no change to network topology or edge strengths.
quote: By applying standard approaches from behavioral theory [17], it was seen that even simple models of gene regulatory networks (GRNs) and molecular pathways show several different kinds of learning, including habituation, sensitization, and Pavlovian (associative) conditioning [23, 24].
scope: Computational models of gene regulatory networks and molecular pathways (cited work from the author's group, refs [23, 24])
measurable_quantities: response of a network output node to a conditioned stimulus before and after paired training
response decrement under repeated stimulation (habituation)
candidate_data: Curated ODE models of gene regulatory and signalling networks in BioModels can be re-run under training protocols; time-course expression data in the Gene Expression Omnibus could test it in cells.

label: Planarian heads degenerated by barium regenerate adapted to it via a handful of genes
claim: Planarian flatworms exposed to barium, a nonspecific potassium channel blocker, lose their heads but soon regenerate new heads completely adapted to barium, and transcriptomic analysis shows only a handful of genes up- or down-regulated, which Levin interprets as cells solving a problem in high-dimensional transcriptional space without an evolved response to barium.
quote: Remarkably, they soon regenerate new heads which are completely adapted to the presence of barium [66]. Transcriptomic analysis reveals just a handful of genes that have been up‐ and down‐regulated to enable this feat of morphological and physiological homeostasis.
scope: Planarian flatworms exposed to barium chloride (author's lab's prior work, ref [66])
measurable_quantities: head degeneration and regeneration after barium exposure
number of differentially expressed genes in barium-adapted heads
candidate_data: Planarian transcriptome resources (PlanMine, SmedGD) and any RNA-seq of barium-adapted planaria deposited in the Gene Expression Omnibus.

label: Morphogenesis is behaviour of cell collectives navigating anatomical morphospace
claim: Morphogenesis can be viewed as behaviour in anatomical morphospace: cellular collectives actively navigate from various starting states to the region corresponding to the species-specific target morphology, with competency ranging from a constrained random walk to advanced problem-solving, a framing Levin presents as a useful metaphor for importing tools from behavioural and cognitive science.
quote: We previously argued that morphogenesis can be viewed as behavior in anatomical morphospace [13]; on this model, cellular collectives are systems that actively navigate from various starting states to a region corresponding to the species‐specific target morphology (Figure 2).
scope: Developing and regenerating multicellular organisms
candidate_data: none known

label: Anatomical homeostasis uses large-scale feedback loops that reduce error from a target
claim: Morphogenetic problem-solving cases indicate that anatomical development is not entirely open-loop: large-scale feedback loops measure distance from a target anatomical state and execute diverse molecular steps to reduce the error, and such networks can store setpoints that are complex data structures rather than simple scalars.
quote: These examples indicate that these processes are not entirely open‐loop: large‐scale feedback loops exist that measure distance from a given target state and execute diverse molecular steps to implement those goals (reduce error).
scope: Regulative development and regeneration in animals (e.g. the cases in the paper's Table 1)
measurable_quantities: final anatomy after perturbations of different size and type
termination of growth or remodelling when target anatomy is reached
candidate_data: Regeneration and morphometric time-course image data such as in the Image Data Resource or Dryad; no single dataset measures the setpoint directly.

label: Channelopathies that cause patterning defects link developmental biology and neuroscience
claim: The deep symmetry between developmental biology and neuroscience is shown by the many ion-channel diseases (channelopathies) that produce patterning defects, and by the applicability of neuroscience tools, from drugs to optogenetics to training protocols, to morphogenetic decisions.
quote: It can be seen in numerous channelopathies that result in patterning defects (see Table 1 in [110], and [111, 112, 113]), and in the applicability of the tools of neuroscience—from drugs to optogenetics to training protocols—to morphogenetic decisions.
scope: Vertebrates including humans; ion channel genes and developmental phenotypes
measurable_quantities: frequency of morphological or craniofacial phenotypes among ion channel gene mutations
developmental effects of neuroactive drugs and optogenetic stimulation
candidate_data: Human genotype–phenotype databases (OMIM, ClinVar, HPO annotations) and model-organism phenotype databases (MGI, ZFIN, Xenbase) for ion channel genes.

label: An endogenous electric face of resting potentials determines vertebrate face patterning
claim: An endogenous spatial distribution of resting membrane potentials (the 'electric face') determines gene expression and anatomical regionalization of the vertebrate face; manipulating it by pharmacology, optogenetics or ion channel misexpression predictably changes craniofacial development and explains why ion channel mutations cause craniofacial phenotypes from frog to human.
quote: One example is the electric face (Figure 4B)—an endogenous distribution of resting potentials that determines the gene expression and anatomical regionalization of the vertebrate face [118].
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos, generalized to vertebrates including humans (author's lab's prior work, refs [118, 119])
measurable_quantities: spatial pattern of resting membrane potential (voltage-dye imaging) in the craniofacial region
craniofacial morphology and regional marker expression after manipulating it
candidate_data: Xenbase expression and phenotype data for Xenopus craniofacial development; human channelopathy craniofacial phenotypes in OMIM.

label: A membrane-voltage change can induce eyes almost anywhere in the Xenopus body
claim: In Xenopus laevis, misexpressing potassium channels to change membrane voltage induces ectopic eyes in many posterior regions including the gut, showing that cells outside the anterior neural field are competent to build eyes when given a higher-level bioelectric signal, contrary to conclusions drawn from prompting cells with the 'master eye gene' Pax6.
quote: It was always thought that cells outside the anterior neural field in vertebrates were not competent to build eyes. But prior studies prompted cells with the so‐called master eye gene Pax6 [123]. It turns out that a higher‐level signal (V mem change) can induce eyes almost anywhere in the body.
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos injected with potassium channel mRNA (author's lab's prior work, ref [120])
measurable_quantities: incidence and location of ectopic eyes after ion channel misexpression
membrane potential of injected cells
candidate_data: Xenbase phenotype and expression data; image data from the original Xenopus ectopic-eye studies if deposited.

label: Many ectopic eye spots but one eye reflect competing goals of neighbouring cell groups
claim: In Xenopus embryos injected with a potassium channel, many ectopic eye spots appear early but typically only one new eye forms; Levin interprets this as bidirectional signalling between channel-induced cells pushed toward an eye setpoint, which recruit neighbours, and uninjected neighbours whose setpoint is still 'gut', which signal to maintain normal fate.
quote: At early stages in embryos injected with the potassium channel, many ectopic eye spots are detected, but just one new eye tends to appear at the end. This is the consequence of conversation between morphogenetic agents with different goals.
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos misexpressing potassium channels
measurable_quantities: number of early ectopic eye-marker spots versus final ectopic eyes per embryo
signals exchanged between injected and uninjected cells
candidate_data: Time-lapse imaging and marker expression data in Xenopus (Xenbase for marker genes); the signals are stated to be unidentified.

label: Restoring the neural-plate bioelectric prepattern rescues teratogen and Notch defects
claim: Normal brain morphogenesis in vertebrate (frog) embryos depends on a specific bioelectric prepattern that chemical or genetic teratogens alter; forcing a return to the correct prepattern in the neural plate, for example by activating the HCN2 channel, corrects brain morphology, gene expression and learning capacity in animals exposed to alcohol, nicotine or a dominant Notch mutation.
quote: Forcing a return to the correct prepattern in the neural plate can correct brain morphology, gene expression, and learning capacity in animals exposed to alcohol, nicotine, or even mutations of the critical neurogenesis gene Notch [124, 125, 126].
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos exposed to alcohol, nicotine or Notch mutation (author's lab's prior work, refs [124–126])
measurable_quantities: neural-plate membrane potential pattern
brain morphology, marker gene expression and learning performance after rescue
candidate_data: Xenbase expression data for brain markers; behavioural and morphological data from the original Xenopus rescue studies if deposited.

label: The same electroceutical, monensin, induces tails at tail wounds and legs at leg wounds
claim: Applied systemically, the same bioelectric-modifying drug (monensin) triggers tail regeneration at tail wounds and leg regeneration at leg wounds, showing that the specificity of the regenerative response lies in the responding cell collective rather than in the reagent.
quote: Even more remarkably, the exact same electroceutical—monensin—triggers tails in tail wounds and legs at leg wounds: the specificity in all of these cases is in the cell collective that responds to the stimulus [128, 200].
scope: Amphibian (Xenopus) tadpole tail and limb regeneration (author's lab's prior work, refs [128, 200])
measurable_quantities: regeneration rate of tails and limbs after systemic monensin exposure
identity of the regenerated structure per wound site
candidate_data: Xenopus regeneration data in Xenbase and published tadpole regeneration scoring data; none known as a deposited dataset.

label: Cancer cells are not more selfish; they have smaller selves
claim: On the cognitive light cone model of cancer, in which the 'cognitive light cone' is the spatiotemporal size of the homeodynamic goal states a system can pursue, cancer is a pathological rolling back to small cell-level goals: cancer cells are not more selfish but have smaller selves, treating the rest of the body as external environment.
quote: But more specifically, the cognitive light cone model suggests that cancer cells are not more selfish; they just have smaller selves.
scope: Cancer in multicellular animals
measurable_quantities: spatial extent of physiological coupling of tumour cells with host tissue
range of variables regulated by transformed versus normal cells
candidate_data: Tumour gap-junction (connexin) expression and electrophysiology data, e.g. TCGA expression of connexin genes; no dataset measures goal-state size directly.

label: Gap-junction closure in transformation is a positive feedback loop of isolation
claim: Cells may physiologically disconnect from the tissue network (e.g. closing gap junctions under prolonged stress), and each reduction in connectivity makes local computation easier and further gap-junction closure more likely, a positive feedback loop of dissociation that makes tissue-level goals ever harder to achieve; Levin presents this as consistent with gap-junction closure in early transformation and with tumours induced by non-carcinogenic geometric barriers.
quote: Each reduction in physiological connectivity makes it easier for cells to perform computations at the local level. This makes it easier for cells to close off gap junctions even more, driving a positive feedback loop—a cycle of dissociation and isolation that makes it ever harder to achieve large‐scale cell collective goals (maintaining complex anatomical structure).
scope: Early carcinogenic transformation in animal tissues
measurable_quantities: gap-junctional coupling over the course of transformation
connexin expression in pre-neoplastic versus normal tissue
candidate_data: Connexin (GJA1 and related) expression across tumour stages in TCGA and the Gene Expression Omnibus; dye-coupling measurements would need new data.

label: Oncogene-induced cancer can be detected early by bioelectrical imaging
claim: Cancer induced in vivo by human oncogenes can be detected early by bioelectrical (membrane-voltage) imaging, as predicted by the view of cancer as a failure of bioelectric 'cognitive glue'.
quote: It has now been shown that (a) cancer induced by human oncogenes in vivo can be detected early by bioelectrical imaging [175]
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos expressing human oncogenes (author's lab's prior work, ref [175])
measurable_quantities: membrane potential of oncogene-expressing cells before tumour formation
predictive accuracy of voltage imaging for later tumour formation
candidate_data: Voltage-dye imaging data from the original Xenopus oncogene studies if deposited; Xenbase.

label: Transient bioelectric and serotonergic perturbation induces a melanoma-like phenotype
claim: Transient perturbation of bioelectrical and serotonergic signalling among cells can induce a melanoma-like phenotype in the absence of carcinogens, oncogenes or DNA damage.
quote: (b) transient perturbation of bioelectrical and serotonergic signaling among cells can induce a melanoma‐like phenotype in the absence of carcinogens, oncogenes, or DNA damage [176, 177, 178]
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos and their melanocytes (author's lab's prior work, refs [176–178])
measurable_quantities: melanocyte number, shape and invasiveness after depolarization of instructor cells
serotonin signalling activity
candidate_data: Xenbase and any deposited transcriptomes of hyperpigmented Xenopus in the Gene Expression Omnibus.

label: Oncogene-induced tumours can be prevented and normalized by managing bioelectric state
claim: Tumours induced by powerful human oncogenes can be prevented and normalized by managing their bioelectric state (e.g. forcing hyperpolarization), without correcting the oncogene.
quote: (c) tumors induced by powerful human oncogenes can be prevented and normalized by managing their bioelectric state [175, 179, 180, 181]
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos expressing human oncogenes such as KRAS (author's lab's prior work, refs [175, 179–181])
measurable_quantities: tumour incidence with and without hyperpolarizing ion channel expression or drugs
membrane potential of oncogene-expressing cells
candidate_data: Xenbase; tumour-incidence counts in the original studies' supplementary data.

label: Physiological information processing, not genetic hardware, dominates cancer outcomes
claim: Levin interprets the ability to normalize oncogene-driven tumours by restoring bioelectric connectivity (reinflating cells' cognitive light cone) as showing that physiological information processing, not genetic hardware, dominates cancer outcomes, suggesting a clinical roadmap different from chemotherapy.
quote: This ability to reinflate the cognitive light cone of cells shows that physiological information processing, not genetic hardware, dominates outcomes and suggests a clinical roadmap quite different from the chemotherapy that dominates the field today [165, 168, 182].
scope: Cancer in animals, with clinical implications for humans
measurable_quantities: tumour outcome as a function of bioelectric state versus mutational load
candidate_data: Ion channel drug repurposing and tumour outcome data (e.g. DepMap drug sensitivity, TCGA ion channel expression); none known that directly compares the two causes.

label: Planaria have chaotic genomes yet regenerate, resist cancer and do not age
claim: Planaria, despite chaotic mixoploid genomes from ~400 million years of asexual reproduction and large numbers of plastic proliferative stem cells, are champions of regeneration, cancer resistant and apparently do not age, the opposite of what a 'genome drives function' paradigm would predict.
quote: Despite that, they are champions of regeneration, are cancer resistant, and apparently do not age. This is the polar opposite of the outcome that the current paradigm of “genome drives function” would predict for the animal with the messiest genome, full of undifferentiated cells in the adult stage.
scope: Asexual planarian flatworms (e.g. Schmidtea mediterranea asexual strain)
measurable_quantities: somatic genome heterogeneity and ploidy
regeneration capacity
tumour incidence
age-related decline
candidate_data: Planarian genome and single-cell resources (SmedGD, PlanMine) and published karyotype/ploidy data for asexual strains.

label: Embryos in large groups form a 'hyperembryo' that resists teratogens better
claim: Individual embryos raised in large groups form a kind of 'hyperembryo' with its own distinct transcriptome and an ability to resist teratogenic challenges far better than individual embryos or small groups.
quote: For example, the hypothesis of scale‐free biology [196] has led to the discovery that individual embryos in large groups form a kind of “hyperembryo” with its own unique transcriptome and an ability to solve teratogenic challenges far better than individual embryos (or small groups) exhibit [197].
scope: Groups of Xenopus laevis embryos (author's lab's prior work, ref [197])
measurable_quantities: malformation rate after teratogen exposure as a function of group size
transcriptome differences between grouped and isolated embryos
candidate_data: RNA-seq of grouped versus isolated embryos if deposited in the Gene Expression Omnibus; Xenbase.

label: Aging may result from degraded bioelectric pattern memories that maintain tissue order
claim: Levin proposes that aging is due to the degradation of endogenous bioelectric pattern memories required throughout life to maintain tissue order, so that solutions to aging need to target this information scaffold as well as cell-level rejuvenation (e.g. Yamanaka factors).
quote: we have previously proposed that aging is due to the degradation of important endogenous (bioelectric) pattern memories that are required throughout the lifespan to maintain tissue order [146, 147].
scope: Aging tissues in multicellular animals
measurable_quantities: spatial order of resting membrane potential patterns in young versus old tissue
age-related change in ion channel and gap-junction expression
candidate_data: Aging transcriptome atlases such as Tabula Muris Senis for ion channel and connexin expression with age; voltage-pattern data would need new measurements.

label: Physarum learns and decides without neurons, and its behaviour is its morphological change
claim: The unicellular slime mould Physarum learns from repeated experience and makes decisions (e.g. growing towards the heavier of distant inert objects) without a brain, neurons or cellularization, and in Physarum behaviour is implemented as change of body shape, blurring the distinction between morphological and behavioural problems.
quote: These examples of learning and decision-making occur in the absence of a brain, neurons, or cellularization. From the perspective of evolutionary change across behavioral domains, one interesting thing is that for Physarum, its behavior is its morphological change.
scope: Physarum polycephalum (slime mould)
measurable_quantities: habituation to noxious substances over repeated exposures
growth direction relative to object mass
candidate_data: Published Physarum behavioural datasets (e.g. on Dryad or Zenodo, if deposited by the cited studies).

label: Planarian tail fragments regenerate brains that recall trained behaviour
claim: Tail fragments of planarian flatworms trained on specific tasks regenerate into animals that show recall of the trained information, so behavioural memories are apparently imprinted onto the new brain as it forms, linking the information processing that restores body shape with that which preserves past experience.
quote: Tails of worms trained on specific tasks regenerate into animals that show recall of the original information: the behavioral memories are apparently also imprinted onto the new brain as it forms (McConnell et al. 1959; Shomrat and Levin 2013).
scope: Planarian flatworms (McConnell 1959; Shomrat and Levin 2013 with Dugesia japonica)
measurable_quantities: trained-task performance (e.g. latency or savings) of regenerates from trained versus naive worms
candidate_data: Automated planarian behaviour datasets from the cited studies if deposited; otherwise new training experiments.

label: Xenopus tadpoles with only a tail eye can see through it
claim: Xenopus laevis tadpoles produced with no primary eyes and a single eye on the tail can see out of the ectopic eye, which can connect to the spinal cord, showing that a frog's cellular hardware can adapt within one generation to a radical reconfiguration of its visual system.
quote: Tadpoles of the frog Xenopus laevis can be produced with no primary eyes, but one eye on their tails; these animals can see out of an ectopic eye, which can connect to the spinal cord (Blackiston and Levin 2013).
scope: Xenopus laevis tadpoles with transplanted ectopic eyes (author's lab, Blackiston and Levin 2013)
measurable_quantities: performance on visual learning assays
innervation of the spinal cord by the ectopic optic nerve
candidate_data: Behavioural data from Blackiston and Levin 2013 if deposited; Xenbase.

label: Bioelectric network information cannot be read from transcript or protein levels
claim: Because ion channels open and close post-translationally, the same channels can yield different voltage states depending on cell history and different channels can yield the same voltage map, the information content of a bioelectric network cannot be read out at the transcriptional or proteomic level and must be studied in living tissue.
quote: As a corollary, the information content of this network cannot be read out at the transcriptional or even proteomic level: channels open and close post-translationally, and the same channels can give rise to different voltage states depending on cells’ history, while diverse channels can give rise to the exact same voltage map.
scope: Bioelectric networks of neural and non-neural cells
measurable_quantities: correlation between ion channel transcript/protein profiles and measured resting potential across cells
candidate_data: Patch-seq datasets pairing electrophysiology with transcriptomes (e.g. Allen Cell Types Database) and voltage imaging paired with single-cell RNA-seq.

label: Bioelectric networks are a cognitive glue that enlarges the cognitive light cone of cells
claim: Bioelectric networks, through their plasticity, multiscale historicity (memory) and learning capacity, act as a 'cognitive glue' that binds the cybernetic goal-directedness of single cells into a higher-order system pursuing larger-scale goals (a larger cognitive light cone), and this capacity is not unique to brains.
quote: Bioelectric networks, with their inherent plasticity, multiscale historicity, and learning capacity, are an ideal kind of “cognitive glue” that binds the primitive goal-directedness (in the cybernetic sense) of single cells into a higher order system with a larger cognitive light cone (Fig. 1E).
scope: Neural and non-neural cell collectives in multicellular organisms
measurable_quantities: effect of disrupting gap-junctional or bioelectric coupling on the spatial scale of coordinated patterning or repair
candidate_data: Gap-junction blocker and connexin mutant phenotype data in model organisms (ZFIN, MGI, Xenbase); no dataset measures goal scale directly.

label: Neural bioelectric machinery was an evolutionary pivot from navigating morphospace
claim: Ion channels, gap junctions and neurotransmitters were originally used to control cell behaviours toward morphogenetic outcomes (navigating anatomical morphospace); their use to drive 3D behaviour via muscle is an evolutionary pivot, exapted with a speed-up from hours to milliseconds and a shift from spatial to temporal (spiking) patterns, and this conservation is why neuroscience tools work throughout the body.
quote: The current use of these components to implement behaviors in 3D space by controlling muscle activity represents an evolutionary pivot: their original usage was to navigate anatomical morphospace (Fields et al. 2020) (that is, to control all cell behaviors toward specific morphogenetic outcomes).
scope: Evolution of animal nervous systems from non-neural bioelectric signalling
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic distribution and developmental roles of ion channel, connexin/innexin and neurotransmitter genes in non-neural lineages
candidate_data: Comparative genomics of ion channel and gap-junction gene families across early-branching animals and unicellular relatives (e.g. Ensembl Metazoa, UniProt).

label: Morphogenetic pattern memory habituates: repeatedly amputated axolotl limbs stop regrowing
claim: The anatomical setpoint that guides regeneration is a pattern memory that is stable but modifiable by experience; for example, repeated amputation of axolotl limbs leads the tissue to habituate to the loss and eventually stop trying to regrow.
quote: This pattern memory can, like any good memory, be modified by experience (it is stable, but also labile to the right kinds of stimuli). For example, repeated amputation of axolotl limbs leads to the tissue habituating to the loss of limb and eventually giving up trying to re-grow (Bryant et al. 2017).
scope: Axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) limb regeneration and regenerating animals generally
measurable_quantities: regeneration success versus number of repeated amputations
candidate_data: Repeated-amputation data from Bryant et al. 2017 if deposited; axolotl genomic and transcriptomic resources (e.g. the Axolotl-omics portal).

label: Deer antlers re-form an ectopic branch at a past injury site year after year
claim: In deer trophic memory, an ectopic branch is formed in the otherwise stereotyped antler at the location of earlier damage year after year, long after the damaged rack has been shed, a memory of 3D position held by scalp cells that regenerate the antler annually.
quote: Trophic memory in deer (Bubenik and Pavlansky 1965; Lobo et al. 2014) enables an ectopic branch in their otherwise stereotypical antler structure to be formed year after year, at a specific point of earlier damage, long after the damaged antler rack has been shed
scope: Deer (Cervidae) antler regeneration
measurable_quantities: recurrence of ectopic tines at injury sites across successive antler cycles
candidate_data: Historical antler morphology records (Bubenik and Pavlansky 1965) and the data compiled by Lobo et al. 2014; none known as a deposited dataset.

label: Bioelectrically induced two-headed planaria stay two-headed across later regenerations
claim: In planarian flatworms the number of heads a regenerating fragment builds is set by the state of a bioelectric circuit with a default of one; transiently modifying it re-sets it to 'two', and the resulting two-headed worms keep regenerating as two-headed through multiple rounds of cutting without further manipulation, unless the pattern is experimentally reset.
quote: Remarkably, when cut again in multiple subsequent rounds of regeneration (with no further manipulation), the fragments continue to result in two-headed animals. This shift in the target morphology for regeneration is permanent (unless the animal’s bioelectric pattern memory is reset back to a one-headed state by an experimental manipulation).
scope: Planarian flatworms (Dugesia japonica), author's lab (Oviedo et al. 2010; Durant et al. 2019)
measurable_quantities: fraction of two-headed regenerates across successive amputation rounds
anterior–posterior membrane potential pattern
candidate_data: Planarian resources PlanMine and SmedGD for gene expression; regeneration scoring data from the original studies if deposited.

label: Planarian head number is not directly encoded in the genome
claim: How many heads a planarian cellular collective produces is not directly encoded in its genome, since the same wild-type cells can produce 1-, 2- or 0-headed planaria depending on their history; the genome encodes the hardware (e.g. ion channels) while the outcome results from experience-sensitive electrophysiological 'software'.
quote: The question, of how many heads a given cellular collective will produce, is, surprisingly, not directly encoded in its genome because exactly the same, wild-type set of cells can produce 1-, 2-, or 0-headed planaria depending on their history.
scope: Planarian flatworms
measurable_quantities: genomic differences (if any) between one- and two-headed lines derived from the same wild-type stock
candidate_data: Planarian genome assemblies (SmedGD, PlanMine) and resequencing of two-headed lines if available.

label: Genetic assimilation of bioelectric phenotypes likely shaped body-plan evolution
claim: Evolutionary changes in ion channel properties that lead to genetic assimilation of bioelectrically induced phenotypes are likely an important aspect of the evolution of body plans and other morphological features, analogous to the Baldwin effect for learning.
quote: Evolutionary tweaks of ion channel properties that eventually lead to genetic assimilation of bioelectrically induced phenotypes is likely an important aspect of the evolution of body plans and other morphological features, much as the Baldwin effect is thought to be a key dynamic for the role of cognition and learning in evolutionary lineages (Baldwin 1896).
scope: Evolution of animal body plans
measurable_quantities: association between ion channel sequence or expression divergence and morphological divergence among species
whether bioelectrically induced phenotypes become heritable under selection
candidate_data: Comparative genomics of ion channel genes (Ensembl, UniProt) combined with morphological trait databases; assimilation experiments would need new data.

label: Commensal bacteria can hijack planarian morphogenesis to cause two-headed regeneration
claim: Like parasites that manipulate host neurobehavioural systems, commensal bacteria can override the default planarian morphogenetic control system and cause two-headed regeneration.
quote: the planarian morphogenetic control system too can be hijacked not only by bioengineers (as described above) but also by commensal bacteria which can over-ride the default system and lead to two-headed regeneration (Williams et al. 2020).
scope: Planarian flatworms and their commensal microbiota (Williams et al. 2020)
measurable_quantities: two-headed regeneration rate with altered versus normal microbiome
candidate_data: 16S rRNA microbiome sequencing of planaria in the Sequence Read Archive if deposited by Williams et al. 2020.

label: A latent two-head bioelectric pattern is a counterfactual memory of the future target form
claim: Because a two-headed bioelectric pattern can exist in an anatomically normal one-headed planarian with normal gene expression, the bioelectric pattern is not a readout of current anatomy but a representation of the target morphology to be built if the animal is injured, in effect a counterfactual memory.
quote: In the case of a two-headed pattern in a one-headed host, this means that the bioelectrical pattern is not a read-out of what the anatomy is currently, but rather a representation of what it should be, weeks later, following regeneration if the animal is injured.
scope: Planarian flatworms with altered bioelectric patterns (Durant et al. 2017)
measurable_quantities: membrane potential pattern in intact worms
head number of their regenerates after amputation
candidate_data: Voltage-dye imaging and regeneration outcome data from the original planarian studies if deposited; PlanMine for expression data.

label: Ion channel drugs can make planarian head number flip stochastically at each regeneration
claim: Exposure to ion channel drugs can put the planarian bioelectric circuit into a bistable state in which, at each regeneration, fragments of these 'cryptic' worms randomly regenerate as one-headed or two-headed, analogous to bistability in perceptual systems.
quote: Exposure to ion channel drugs (a physiological experience akin to electrical signals from a retina or other sense organ, not a genetic change) can place the bioelectric circuit into a state in which it cannot decide between two outcomes and flips back and forth stochastically at each regenerative event (recall of target morphology).
scope: Planarian flatworms treated with ion channel or gap-junction drugs (Durant et al. 2017)
measurable_quantities: fraction of one- versus two-headed regenerates over successive cuts of the same lineage
candidate_data: Regeneration scoring data from Durant et al. 2017 if deposited; none known otherwise.

label: Transient gap-junction blockade makes planarian fragments build heads of other species
claim: Temporary exposure of planarian fragments to a blocker of electrical synapses (gap junctions) causes them to build head shapes of other planarian species 100–150 million years distant, with no genetic change; Levin interprets this as the bioelectric network navigating to other attractors in morphospace, and the worms later remodel back to normal.
quote: One example of this plasticity of morphogenetic behavior (expanding on the default genetically encoded repertoire) is the fact that temporary exposure to a blocker of electrical synapses (i.e., an anesthetic) causes planarian fragments to create the heads of other species, with no genetic change required (Emmons-Bell et al. 2015; Sullivan et al. 2016).
scope: Planarian flatworms (Girardia dorotocephala and related species), author's lab (Emmons-Bell et al. 2015)
measurable_quantities: head shape morphometrics of regenerates after gap-junction blockade compared with other species
time to remodel back to native shape
candidate_data: Head morphometric data from Emmons-Bell et al. 2015 if deposited; planarian phylogenies and species images.

label: Newt kidney tubules keep normal diameter with fewer, larger cells, down to one cell
claim: In newts whose embryonic cells are made larger (e.g. by polyploidy), kidney tubules use fewer cells to keep the normal tubule diameter and body size, and with enormous cells a single cell bends around itself to form the tubule, showing that different molecular mechanisms are called on to reach the same large-scale anatomical goal.
quote: However, if the cells of the early embryo are artificially made to be larger, fewer cells will be used, resulting in the same (normal) tubule diameter and overall body size. Remarkably, this can be pushed to a fascinating extreme: if the cells are made to be enormous, a single cell will bend around itself, producing the normal size tubule diameter.
scope: Polyploid newt embryos (Fankhauser 1945)
measurable_quantities: cells per tubule cross-section versus ploidy
tubule diameter and body size
candidate_data: Fankhauser's historical histological measurements; new data from polyploid amphibians would be needed.

label: Xenobots perform kinematic self-replication not known in any other species
claim: Xenobots, proto-organisms that form spontaneously from dissociated frog embryo skin cells, are motile via cilia and perform kinematic self-replication, building copies of themselves from loose cells in the medium, a novel solution reached within 48 h without any evolutionary history of selection as Xenobots.
quote: The most remarkable novel behavior is that of kinematic self-replication: Xenobots build copies of themselves by rearranging loose cells provided to them in the medium. This is Von Neumann-style replication that is not, to our knowledge, used by any other species on Earth.
scope: Xenobots made from Xenopus laevis embryonic ectoderm (Kriegman et al. 2021a)
measurable_quantities: number of offspring aggregates formed per parent
generations of replication sustained
candidate_data: Data and code deposited with the Xenobot self-replication study (Kriegman et al. 2021, PNAS) if available on Zenodo or GitHub.

label: Scrambled Xenopus tadpole faces reach a normal frog face by new paths
claim: During metamorphosis, Xenopus laevis tadpoles reach the correct frog face configuration not only from a normal tadpole configuration but also from a wide range of experimentally scrambled craniofacial configurations, using new paths through morphospace that end in the same goal region.
quote: For example, during metamorphosis, the tadpole of Xenopus laevis can reach the correct frog face region of morphospace not only from its default starting position (a normal tadpole configuration), but also from a wide range of scrambled configurations (Vandenberg et al. 2012)—using new paths through that morphospace that nevertheless end up in the same goal region (Friston et al. 2015; Pezzulo and Levin 2016).
scope: Xenopus laevis tadpoles with induced craniofacial malformations (author's lab, Vandenberg et al. 2012)
measurable_quantities: craniofacial organ positions before and after metamorphosis
fraction of scrambled tadpoles reaching normal frog face
candidate_data: Craniofacial morphometric data from Vandenberg et al. 2012 if deposited; Xenbase.

label: A few bioelectrically induced lens cells recruit host cells to build a normal-sized lens
claim: When an ectopic lens is induced in tail tissue by bioelectric modulation, misexpressing the ion channel in only a small subset of the needed cells suffices: these cells recruit unmodified host cells to reach the critical mass for a normal-sized lens, so downstream modules such as size control are activated without micromanagement.
quote: For example, when an ectopic lens (in tail tissue) is induced by bioelectric modulation, it is sufficient to misexpress the channel only in a small subset of the needed cells: once their organ-level goal is specified, these cells will secondarily recruit other (un-modified) host cells as needed to achieve the critical mass needed to produce a normal-sized lens.
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos with ion channel misexpression in tail tissue
measurable_quantities: fraction of lens cells derived from injected (lineage-labelled) versus host cells
lens size versus number of injected cells
candidate_data: Lineage-tracing image data from the original Xenopus ectopic-eye studies if deposited; Xenbase.

label: Gap junctions wipe ownership of memory molecules, partly erasing cell individuality
claim: By directly connecting the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells, gap junctions provide an 'owner wiping property' for stress signals and other molecular traces of experience (e.g. calcium flux), so cells cannot tell whether such a signal is their own or a neighbour's; this partly erases individual cell identity and lets the collective scale up measurements, stored goals and actions.
quote: Second, by providing direct connections between the intracellular milieus of cells, they provide an “owner wiping property” for stress signals and other molecular traces of experience: cells cannot tell whether a given memory molecule (e.g., calcium flux) belongs to itself or its neighbors.
scope: Gap-junction-coupled cells in morphogenetic and neural tissues
measurable_quantities: intercellular spread of calcium or other second messengers through gap junctions
coordination of cell responses with and without gap-junction coupling
candidate_data: Calcium-imaging datasets of coupled tissues (e.g. on the Image Data Resource or Zenodo) and connexin mutant phenotypes in MGI and ZFIN.
